Verification report — PyTorch ports vs the original code

bsce, October 2026. All numbers come from tests/results/equivalence.jsonl (written by the pytest suite) and can be regenerated with python -m pytest tests -q followed by python scripts/summarize_tests.py.

1. Summary

Every component used in the LADMM project was re-implemented in Python/PyTorch and compared with the original code run unchanged on identical inputs: MATLAB code in GNU Octave 8.4, the TF-1 training graphs through tf.compat.v1 (TensorFlow 2.21, CPU), and THADMM-Net in PyTorch.

Two results need care when you use the PyTorch training (sections 6 and 7): GM-LAMP trained from its original initial value is not reproducible bit-for-bit by any implementation (including TF on another device), and float32 training agrees only statistically. Both are properties of the original method / precision, not of the port.

2. How the comparison is done

  • Original code is not edited. Interventions are limited to (i) Octave shims for rand, randn, normrnd that replay a stream of numbers given by the test (tests/harness/octave_shims), (ii) a module that maps import tensorflow to tf.compat.v1 and supplies tf.contrib.distributions.percentile for the ALISTA code (tests/harness/tf1_shim.py), (iii) recording the indices returned by np.random.choice in the training loops, and (iv) derived copies with Python-3 syntax or float32→float64 for code that is float32 by design (tests/harness/make_reference_copies.py; the copies are regenerated from the originals and differ only in those tokens).
  • Inputs: random SV channels at several SNRs and seeds; for networks, the authors' trained weights where they exist, and otherwise the original initial values plus a random perturbation (so that no parameter sits at a special value that could hide an error).
  • Metric: relative Frobenius error ‖a−b‖/‖b‖. With float64 on both sides the expected level is 1e-16 … 2e-13 (round-off accumulated through up to 16 layers and Adam steps).
  • Most checks run on several seeds / SNRs / arrays (column n of the tables, 1–32 cases per check); the suites were run several times while the code was developed. Final full run: 192 passed, 1 skipped by design (see §11), 58 min on two CPU cores (tests/logs/full_suite.log).

5. Training graphs (forward, gradients, optimiser)

For each original training script the TF graph is built by the script's own functions (build_LAMP + setup_training, build_LADMM + setup_training, ...). The PyTorch model gets the same weights; then the test compares (a) every layer output, (b) the stage list and the variable list of every stage, (c) the gradient of every stage loss with respect to every variable, and (d) the parameters after several Adam steps of every stage.

Details that had to be reproduced to reach these numbers: the gradient routing of tf.maximum at ties, TF-1's Adam (Eigen update order; hyper-parameters and the beta-power accumulators are float32 even in float64 graphs — ignoring this gives 3e-6 instead of 5e-15), TF's percentile with banker's rounding (ALISTA support selection), and the row-major reshapes of the Kronecker operator.

6. Training loops end to end

tests/test_training_loop_vs_tf.py runs the original do_training loop (data loading, validation every iv1 steps before the step, round(nmse, 5), early stopping every 100·iv1 steps, a fresh Adam per stage, GM-LAMP's warm start of each new layer from the previous one) on small data (600 training / 100 validation channels, maxit 200–300, better_wait 30–40, T = 2–3) and records the minibatch indices it draws and the parameters it saves after every stage. The bsce Trainer is fed the same minibatches.

case (script) stages steps iteration counts max NMSE diff. per stage max param. diff.

GM-LAMP, spread initial value, T=2 16 4816 all equal 4.7e-07 dB 4.0e-14
GM-LAMP, original initial value, T=2 16 3013 all equal 5.0e-07 dB (stages 1–12), 1.5e-02 dB after 5.6e-16 (stages 1–9), see §7
LADMM full, T=2 (A_LADMM_UPA_SV_0_20dB.py) 16 3113 all equal 4.8e-07 dB 1.2e-15
LADMM Kronecker, T=2 (C_UPA_DeepMIMO_0_10dB_Kronecker.py) 16 3216 all equal 4.3e-07 dB 2.6e-16
LADMM diagonal, T=2 (A_UPA_DeepMIMO_0_10dB_DiagonalScaling.py) 16 3216 all equal 4.8e-07 dB 3.7e-16

(NMSE differences below 5e-7 dB are the print resolution of the original log, 6 decimals.)

The float32 run is the expected behaviour of single-precision training: TF and PyTorch kernels sum in different orders, the 1e-7 differences of the first steps grow, one early-stop decision flips (stage 12), and the final validation NMSE differs by 0.012 dB. The same happens between two GPUs or two TF versions. For bit-level comparisons use float64 (--set model.precision=float64).

7. GM-LAMP: the original initial value makes training depend on round-off

get_shrinkage_function('gm') initialises every layer with K = 4 identical Gaussian components ([1/K; 0; -1e-9] for every k). With identical components:

  • the gradient that would make the components different is exactly zero in exact arithmetic; in floating point it is round-off (≈1e-16 for the mixture logits);
  • Adam divides by √v, so a round-off-sized gradient produces a non-negligible step, and the symmetric state is unstable: a difference of 1e-16 grows by about ×10 every 8–10 Adam steps.

Consequences seen in the tests:

  1. In the loop test, PyTorch and TF agree to 5.6e-16 for the first 9 stages. From stage 10 ('linear T=2 trainrate=0', when the identical-component layer-1 mixture is trained through layer 2) the layer-1 mixture parameters theta_0 differ by up to 3e-7, without a visible effect on the output while the components are identical (iteration counts equal, NMSE equal to the 6 printed decimals). From stage 13 ('non-linear T=2', layer 2 warm-started from layer 1) the components split differently in the two codes: parameters differ by O(1), final NMSE by 0.015 dB.
  2. Starting PyTorch from TF's state just before stage 13 reproduces TF's split (component weights 0.26904 vs 0.26906 after 100 steps), so the port computes the same dynamics; the outcome depends only on the last bits of the starting point.
  3. tests/diagnostics/gm_symmetry.py trains layer 2 twice from the same state, once with one mean perturbed by 1 part in 1e15. With the original initial value the two runs end O(1) apart (relative difference 1.18) and, in PyTorch on this CPU, the unperturbed run keeps the four components exactly identical for all 400 steps (spread of the means = 0). With the spread initial value the two runs stay 1.9e-15 apart and the components separate (spread 1.16).

The weights shipped with GM-LAMP have clearly different components in every layer (e.g. layer 1 of the SV-ULA 0–10 dB network: weights 0.89 / 0.00 / 0.01 / 0.09), so in the authors' run round-off did break the symmetry. Whether and when it breaks is a matter of the hardware and library, which means a PyTorch GM-LAMP trained from the original value may end up with (nearly) identical components, i.e. effectively a single-Gaussian denoiser.

Recommendation. For GM-LAMP baselines trained with bsce use configs/train/gmlamp_spread.yaml (gm_init: spread: means and log-variances offset by 1e-3·linspace(−1, 1, K)). It changes the initial value by 1e-3, the training is then reproducible (the loop test matches TF to 4e-14 over all stages when both codes get this value), and the components separate through the data. Keep gmlamp_original.yaml for the faithful-reproduction checks, and say in the paper which initialisation was used.

8. Saved models and MATLAB

save_model writes <tag>_<band>.pt (state dict + config + A + training log), <tag>_<band>.mat (all parameters under the original MATLAB names plus model, A, T, cfg_*; read by matlab/bsce_load.m / bsce_infer.m) and, for LAMP / GM-LAMP / LADMM, <tag>_<band>_orig.mat with only the variables the original MATLAB functions read.

check n worst rel. error
.pt and .mat reload in Python; .mat through bsce_infer.m in Octave — all 13 model types 26 1.4e-15
_orig.mat copied to the original file name and run by the unchanged LAMP.m, GM_LAMP.m, LADMM_test.m (LADMM full, Kronecker, proposed kronprior) 10 7.5e-16

_orig.mat exists because the original functions call load(...) inside the function: a weight file that also contains A or T silently replaces the function's own A/T (this is what happens in LADMM_UPA_test.m, see §9).

9. Findings about the original code

  1. GM-LAMP initial value — identical mixture components; training outcome depends on round-off (§7).
  2. TF-1 Adam in float64 graphs keeps beta1, beta2, epsilon, the learning rate and the beta-power accumulators in float32. Any re-implementation that uses float64 constants differs by ≈3e-6 per step.
  3. Kronecker LADMM (C_UPA_DeepMIMO_0_10dB_Kronecker.py): the code computes (H2 ⊗ H1) x (row-major reshape), whereas the docstring says H1 ⊗ H2. bsce reproduces the code; for the paper, write the operator the code implements.
  4. LADMM alpha_{T-1} of the last layer never receives a gradient (the last dual update does not reach the output); it stays at its initial value 1. Harmless, but it is counted as a parameter.
  5. Validation rounding: GM-LAMP and the LADMM scripts compare round(nmse, 5); with small NMSE (high SNR, NMSE < 1e-3) 5 decimals are only 2–3 significant digits; ties count as "no improvement" (argmin keeps the first), so early stopping can trigger earlier than the unrounded NMSE would. bsce reproduces it (val_round: 5); the fair protocol uses val_round: null.
  6. LADMM_UPA_test.m hard-codes the depth per SNR range (T = 5 / 4 / 5 / 5) before load(...); the DeepMIMO weight file used for range 1 contains a variable T = 6, which silently overrides the 5 (ranges 2–4 keep 4 / 5 / 5).
  7. DeepMIMO MATLAB evaluation: A is stored in single precision in the DeepMIMO CSmatrix_128256.mat, so A*x and everything after it is computed in single precision (≈1e-7 relative). The tests convert A to double.
  8. genMeasurements leaves trailing all-zero columns when the number of channels is not divisible by the number of SNR chunks; bsce raises an error (strict=False reproduces the original).
  9. Low-rank LADMM initialisation is ill-defined (B_UPA_DeepMIMO_0_10dB_LowRank.py): P, Q are built from the top-r singular vectors of W = (AᵀA + I)⁻¹, but the largest singular value (= 1) has multiplicity N − M = 128 (the null space of A). Which 16 vectors LAPACK returns is arbitrary and differs between MKL (Windows) and OpenBLAS (Linux); the stored golden run differs by 0.28 % in validation NMSE between the two. Runs on one machine are exact.
  10. Uploaded DeepMIMO LADMM weights: with the DeepMIMO test channels and CSmatrix_128256.mat shipped with the GM-LAMP code they give an NMSE of about 0 dB (ULA) and −0.7 … −1.4 dB (UPA) at 2–17 dB SNR, i.e. they were trained with another sensing matrix or other data. The bit-level tests do not depend on this (they compare two implementations with the same weights), but the DeepMIMO results should be regenerated once your DeepMIMO data are uploaded.

10. Pipeline check on CPU (smoke run)

python scripts/run_all.py --scenario configs/scenarios/sv_ula.yaml --smoke generated a tiny SV-ULA data set (1000 / 200 / 200 channels), trained all 14 configurations for both SNR bands (--smoke: maxit 20, T ≤ 2), evaluated them together with AMP and OMP at 11 SNRs (the same noise for all methods, the band network chosen by SNR), and reloaded every saved model (scripts/check_exports.py). The NMSE values are not performance results — 20 iterations on 1000 channels — they only show that every path of the pipeline runs on the CPU.

trained models .pt vs .mat reloaded in Python Octave bsce_infer.m vs PyTorch
float64 (LAMP, GM-LAMP, GM-LAMP-spread, LADMM diag / low-rank / Kronecker) 0 ≤ 1.6e-15
float32 (LADMM full / psd / kronprior / diagprior, LISTA, ALISTA, LVAMP, ADMM-Net) 0 ≤ 6.7e-6 (PyTorch runs in single, MATLAB in double)

.mat files store float64 arrays even for float32-trained networks, so MATLAB evaluates them in double precision (finding 7 in §9 is the same issue in the original DeepMIMO files).

A second file, tests/test_golden.py, trains 13 configurations (every model and LADMM operator except GM-LAMP with the original initial value, whose training is round-off sensitive, §7) for a few iterations in float64 (PyTorch only, ~50 s) and compares with numbers stored in tests/golden/golden.json; two consecutive runs on this machine gave bit-identical results. Run it on your GPU machine (python -m pytest tests/test_golden.py; the GPU is used automatically) to check the installation there (tolerance 1e-7 on GPU, because GPU kernels sum in a different order).

11. Not covered / limits

  • The training loops of the ALISTA repository (utils/train.py), Borgerding's LVAMP and THADMM-Net were not replayed end to end: their data come from in-graph random generators or data loaders that cannot be fed the same minibatches without editing them. Their per-stage operations (forward, gradients, Adam, stage lists) are verified (§5), and the schedule code they share with GM-LAMP/LADMM is covered by §6; the ALISTA schedule (step before validation, per-variable decay) is a port of utils/train.py checked by reading, not by a replay.
  • LISTA, ALISTA and LVAMP are real-valued in their repositories. bsce adds a complex mode for beamspace channels (real weights on Re/Im, shrinkage on |·| with the phase kept). For LISTA/ALISTA the complex mode on real inputs equals the original real code (2.3e-15). For LVAMP the complex mode uses the circular complex Bernoulli-Gaussian prior (with the Wirtinger divergence), which is a different model from the real prior, so that check does not apply (the one skipped test); LVAMP's real mode is the part verified against Borgerding's code.
  • No GPU was available here; all comparisons with the original code used PyTorch on the CPU. tests/test_gpu_vs_cpu.py closes the chain on the GPU machine: for all 14 model configurations, in float64 and float32, it runs the same weights, inputs and minibatches on the CPU and the GPU and compares every stage output, every stage gradient, 5 Adam steps per stage, a short training run (iteration counts, NMSE, final parameters) and the exported .pt/.mat. Tolerances: float64 1e-12 (outputs), 1e-10 (gradients), 1e-9 (Adam), 1e-8 (trained parameters, identical early-stop decisions); float32 at single-precision level and NMSE within 0.1 dB. Then |GPU − original| ≤ |GPU − CPU| + |CPU − original|. Here the file was only dry-run with BSCE_GPU_DEVICE=cpu (code path check). TF32 is disabled on CUDA so float32 matmuls stay in full single precision. GM-LAMP from the original initial value is compared only statistically in training (§7).
  • DeepMIMO: scenario files are prepared (configs/scenarios/deepmimo_*.yaml); the data will be produced with generate_data.py --measurements-only once the channels are uploaded.
